sections.title: Flexible cords and cables — article intro
sections.plain_explanation: Article 400 covers cords and flexible cables used to connect equipment, not wire that is installed as part of a building. It sorts cord types by construction and permitted use, and it draws a hard line against using a cord as a substitute for permanent wiring. If the wire is meant to stay in the building, it belongs in a Chapter 3 wiring method, not in a cord.
sections.on_the_job: When you reach for a cord, ask whether the equipment is meant to move, be serviced, or be exchanged. If the answer is no, run a permanent wiring method instead. Check the cord jacket marking for the type letter before you trust it in a damp or hard-use location.

sections.title: Uses permitted and not permitted — flexible cords (400.10 / 400.12)
sections.plain_explanation: Sections 400.10 (uses permitted) and 400.12 (uses not permitted) draw the line for flexible cords; 400.7 and 400.8 are the 2017 numbers. Permitted uses are the ones that need to move or be serviced: pendants, portable lamps and appliances, elevator and hoist cables, parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections. The not-permitted list is the one that fails inspections: a cord may not substitute for the fixed wiring of a building, run through holes in walls, ceilings, or floors, pass through doorways or windows, attach to building surfaces outside the narrow exceptions, hide inside walls or conduit, or sit where it will be damaged. If a cord is doing a cable's job permanently, it is the wrong wiring method. 400.12, in Code order — flexible cords may not be: (1) a substitute for fixed wiring; (2) run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors; (3) run through doorways, windows or similar openings; (4) attached to building surfaces (except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit); (5) concealed by walls, floors or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings; (6) installed in raceways except as otherwise permitted; (7) installed where subject to physical damage.
sections.on_the_job: The classic callout: an appliance or tool left cord-connected through a wall or across a doorway 'temporarily' for months. If the load is permanent, price and install a real branch circuit — do not dress up a cord run.
sections.figure_idea: Two-column card: 'cord is fine here' scenes (pendant, portable tool) versus 'hardwire it' scenes (through a wall, under a door).

sections.title: What flexible cords may be used for
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 400.10 lists the jobs a flexible cord is allowed to do: hanging fixtures, connecting portable equipment, appliances that need to be moved for cleaning or service, and similar uses where flexibility is the point. The common thread is that the equipment, not the building, is what moves. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box or a permanent load is outside this list.

Cord ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1) for the cord type and the number of current-carrying conductors — the sizes a crew actually holds, figured for two current-carrying conductors:
• 18 AWG cord — 10 A
• 16 AWG cord — 13 A
• 14 AWG cord — 18 A
• 12 AWG cord — 25 A
• 10 AWG cord — 30 A
A third current-carrying conductor in the same cord drops the value (the table's next column), which is why a cord's rating is read off its own table and not off the building-wire ampacity table.
sections.on_the_job: Before you plug or hard-wire a cord to anything, name the 400.10 use out loud. If you cannot name one, stop and run conduit or cable. Watch especially for cords run through walls, ceilings, or doorways, which this article does not allow.

sections.title: Uses not permitted — flexible cords and cables
sections.plain_explanation: Section 400.12 is the stop list for flexible cords and cables — in the 2017 edition this list was numbered 400.8, and the 2020 reorganization of Article 400 moved it here. Unless 400.10 permits the use, a flexible cord, flexible cable, cord set, or power-supply cord may not be used: (1) as a substitute for the fixed wiring of the structure; (2) run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors; (3) run through doorways, windows, or similar openings; (4) attached to building surfaces, except that cords used for temporary wiring under 590.4 may be attached; (5) concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings, except within an enclosure for use in other spaces used for environmental air as permitted by 300.22(C)(3); (6) installed in raceways, except as 400.17 permits in industrial establishments where only qualified persons service the installation; or (7) where it is subject to physical damage. Most failed 'cord' installations fail here, not on ampacity.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, trace the whole cord, not just the ends. If any part of it is stapled, hidden, or passing through a partition, the fix is a permanent wiring method, not a heavier cord.

sections.title: Fixture wires — article intro
sections.plain_explanation: Article 402 covers the small conductors used inside fixtures and equipment, called fixture wires. They are for wiring within a luminaire or similar equipment and for connecting that equipment over a limited distance, not for general branch-circuit runs through a building. Sizes run smaller than branch wiring, which is exactly why they must stay inside the equipment they belong to.
sections.on_the_job: If you find a fixture wire run acting like a branch circuit through a wall or ceiling, flag it. Replace that run with a Chapter 3 method sized for the circuit. Keep fixture-wire splices inside the fixture or its listed outlet box.

sections.title: Fixture wire ampacity — small wire, small numbers (Table 402.5)
sections.plain_explanation:
Fixture wires are the small conductors inside luminaires and equipment, and Table 402.5 gives them their own ampacities — far below what the same gauge carries as a branch conductor. The two sizes crews meet most:
• 18 AWG fixture wire — 6 A
• 16 AWG fixture wire — 8 A
Fixture wire is protected and tapped under the fixture-wire rules (240.5), never treated as branch-circuit wire, and it never leaves the fixture or equipment it belongs to.
sections.on_the_job: Rewiring a fixture whip or a driver lead: match the fixture wire to what the fixture came with. Never extend a circuit with fixture wire because it was handy on the truck.
sections.figure_idea: Gauge ladder: 18 AWG to 6 A, 16 AWG to 8 A, with a red line where branch-circuit wire tables take over.

sections.title: Switches — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 404 covers switches: the devices that open and close a circuit, from a simple single-pole snap switch to motor-circuit switches. It handles which conductor a switch may interrupt, where a grounded (neutral) conductor must be available at a switch box, how high and how accessible a switch must be, and how switch terminals are marked for conductor materials. Start here whenever a switching question is about the device itself rather than the circuit feeding it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 404.1: The switch article's scope now makes clear that wireless controls with no connection to circuit conductors aren't covered, and an informational note sends readers to 210.70. Wireless control gear that never connects to circuit conductors, like a battery-powered remote, falls outside Article 404.
• 404.16: New 404.16 sorts switches into rebuild-allowed and replace-only. Snap switches, dimmers, electronic controls and molded-case switches must be new; knife, butt-contact and bolted pressure switches can be reconditioned. Lighting switches, snap switches of any type, dimmers and electronic control switches like timers can't be reconditioned. Replace them with new devices.
• 404.30: New 404.30: if opening a switch enclosure's door with the switch on would expose bare live parts, the door must need a tool or another approved way to keep unqualified people out. With the switch closed (on), a door that opens onto uninsulated live parts must take a tool to open.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On rough-in, the two 404 questions to settle before the walls close are neutral availability at switch boxes and switch height. Both are cheap at rough-in and expensive after drywall.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: when the plan is silent, Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box. That is a company preference, not an Article 404 requirement.

sections.title: Three-way and four-way switching — what the switch may control
sections.plain_explanation: Section 404.2(A) deals with which conductor a switch interrupts. In plain terms, switching belongs in the ungrounded (hot) conductor, and three-way and four-way arrangements must be wired so the load is never left connected to a hot conductor with the switch appearing to be off in a way that leaves lampholder shells energized. The traveler system exists to let two or more locations control one load while keeping that rule intact.
sections.on_the_job: Wire 3-way/4-way runs by function, not by color habit: common, travelers, switched leg, neutral, ground. Test every switch position at trim and confirm the load is fully controlled from each location before you leave. Never borrow a neutral from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice note (job practice, not code text): label travelers at rough-in when a run is long or passes through several boxes. It saves the trim crew from ringing out pairs.
sections.figure_idea: Figure idea (original, ours): a simple line drawing in our own style showing one load, a 3-way at each end and a 4-way in the middle, with boxes labelled common / travelers / switched leg — no textbook diagram copied.

sections.title: A neutral must be available at most switch locations
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.2(C) requires a grounded conductor — the neutral — to be present at most switch locations in a dwelling and in general lighting control. The reason is practical: modern controls, timers, occupancy sensors, and smart switches often need a neutral to power themselves. There are listed exceptions, including some raceway installations where the neutral can be added later and certain replacement or retrofit situations, so read the exception list for the exact job instead of assuming.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 404.2: One escape hatch for skipping the neutral at lighting switches is gone: a box you can get into later without opening up the finish no longer counts. Gone in 2023: the pass for a switch box reachable later without removing finish materials. Pull the neutral anyway (404.2(C)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, pull the neutral through every switch box even when the planned device is a plain snap switch that does not use it today. Cap it neatly in the back of the box. That one habit prevents the most common 404.2(C) correction and makes later smart-switch work possible without opening walls.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: this is why the Honeywell / ecobee-era control work and smart switches on Sharma jobs assume a neutral in the box. Do not design a switch location that strands a future electronic control without one.

sections.title: Switches in damp or wet locations — and out of the tub/shower wet location
sections.plain_explanation: Article 404 requires switches installed in damp or wet locations to be in enclosures suited to the location, and it separately restricts switches in a bathtub or shower space: a switch may not be installed within the wet location of a tub or shower unless it is part of a listed tub or shower assembly made for that purpose. The rule parallels the receptacle and luminaire zones in 406.9(C) and 410.10(D) — the wettest part of the room is kept free of devices a wet person would operate. A switch on the dry wall outside that space is an ordinary installation.
sections.on_the_job: At layout, treat the tub/shower wet location as a no-switch zone the same way you treat it as a no-receptacle zone. Exterior and patio switches get weatherproof enclosures suited to whether a cover must close over a plug or cord. Pool and spa switching also answers to Article 680 — check Chapter 6 before you place a switch near water.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: outdoor kitchens, lanais, and pool-adjacent switching are damp or wet locations in practice; enclosure choice matters more here than the switch itself.

sections.title: Switches must be reachable — operating handle height
sections.plain_explanation: Section 404.8(A) requires switches to be readily accessible and sets a ceiling on height: the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or working platform. The point is that a person standing on the floor must be able to operate the switch without a ladder or a reach tool. It does not set the normal mounting height for a house switch — that comes from the plan or company practice.
sections.on_the_job: Measure to the handle in its up position, not to the top of the box. Special cases exist for switches next to equipment they serve and for busway-type installations, so check the exceptions before you relocate a switch that looks too high.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: Sharma's default is 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent. The plan governs when it states a height. Do not present 48 in. as a code number — 404.8(A) is the code ceiling, S-05 is our working height.

sections.title: Grounding snap switches (404.9)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 404.9 requires snap switches to be grounded. In practice the switch's metal yoke is bonded through the equipment grounding conductor: a metal box bonded by its EGC grounds the switch through its mounting screws, and in a nonmetallic box the switch's own grounding terminal takes the EGC. The replacement exception matters in old houses: where an existing switch is replaced in a box with no grounding means, the exception's limited paths apply — including GFCI protection or a nonmetallic plate — rather than landing an ungrounded switch and moving on.
sections.on_the_job: On remodels, check for a ground before trim-out, not during the final walk. No EGC in the box changes what devices you may land — flag it at discovery.
sections.figure_idea: Yoke-to-box bond sketch: EGC to a metal box with the switch screws bonding the yoke; green terminal to EGC in a plastic box.

sections.title: Snap switch ratings and the loads they may control
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.14 ties a general-use snap switch to the kind of load it controls. A switch marked for AC only, or for AC/DC, has different limits for motor, inductive, and tungsten-type loads, and a switch may not be loaded past the rating that applies to that load type. In plain terms: the amp number on the yoke is not a promise for every load — the load type decides which limit applies.

The working limits, by load type:
• Resistive loads — up to the switch's full marked ampere rating
• Inductive loads (ballasts, transformers) — full rating on an AC general-use switch; 50 percent of the rating on an AC/DC general-use switch
• Motor loads — 80 percent of the rating on an AC general-use switch, or the switch's marked horsepower rating where it has one
• Tungsten-filament lamp loads — full rating at 120V on an AC general-use snap switch (404.14(A)); the 'T' rating question applies to AC/DC switches (404.14(B))
Worked example: a 15A AC-only snap switch may carry a 12A motor load (15 × 0.80) and up to 15A of tungsten lighting at 120V; the 'T' marking question applies to AC/DC switches.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 404.14: Switch terminals now have wire rules: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Dimmers now follow the same load rule as timers. Push-in (back-stab) holes take only 14 AWG solid copper on a 15-amp circuit, unless the switch is listed and marked for other wire (404.14(D)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the yoke marking before you put a snap switch on a motor, a ballast bank, or a heater. Where the load is a motor or is otherwise hard on contacts, use a switch rated for that duty or control it through a rated contactor or relay.

sections.title: Switch terminal markings for conductor materials (CO/ALR)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 404.15(C) carries the CO/ALR marking rule for switches — the switch-side twin of 406.3(C) for receptacles: a switch designed for the direct connection of aluminum conductors must be marked CO/ALR. The terminal rules that go with the marking, stated for the 2020 NEC in NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122 from the UL guide information for snap switches: terminals of 15A and 20A snap switches are for use with copper and copper-clad aluminum conductors only, unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum; terminals of switches rated 30A and above are for copper only, unless marked AL/CU. Plain aluminum never lands on an unmarked device terminal.
sections.on_the_job: Check the device itself: read the terminal marking on the switch you are holding and match it to the conductor you are landing — no CO/ALR marking, no plain aluminum on the terminal. Do not backstab CCA — Sharma lands CCA on screw terminals only (see S-10).
sections.sharma_note: S-10 applies: CCA is sized one AWG larger than copper and terminations must be listed for the conductor. Never backstab.

sections.title: Receptacles, cord connectors, and attachment plugs — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 406 covers receptacle outlets and the plugs and cord connectors that go into them: how receptacles are rated and grounded, when a replacement must upgrade protection, where face-up devices may be used, what damp and wet locations demand, the tub and shower exclusion zone, and where tamper-resistant receptacles are required. It is the article behind most device-level corrections on a residential final.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.2: One section, 406.2, now holds the no-reconditioning rule for receptacles, cord connectors, plugs and flanged surface devices. The ban itself dates to 2020. None of these four can be reconditioned: receptacles, attachment plugs (caps), cord connectors and flanged surface inlets or outlets.
• 406.3: 406.3(D) now spells out what wire receptacle terminals take: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Push-in (back-stab) holes are for 14 AWG solid copper only, on a 15-amp branch circuit, unless the receptacle is listed and marked for other wire.
• 406.6: Cover plates with a night light or USB charger that draw power through spring contacts on the receptacle screws are now limited to 1 watt and brass or copper alloy screws. A plate whose only connection is spring-tensioned contacts touching the receptacle's terminal screws can't draw more than 1 watt (406.6(D)).
• 406.9: The tub and shower zone now reaches inside and below the tub and gained new exceptions. Weather-resistant listing now covers 30-amp, 50-amp and other wet-location receptacles, and hinged hood covers must open 90 degrees. The zone now covers inside the tub or shower and everything below the rim; a wall, floor, door, window or fixed barrier ends it.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, work 406 as a checklist room by room: correct replacement type, WR where the location needs it, in-use cover where the location is wet, TR where 406.12 requires it, and nothing inside the tub/shower zone.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: points marked GFI on a Sharma plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by the dual-function breaker. Sharma does not install GFCI receptacles as the standard device.

sections.title: Receptacle installation and replacement — the general rules (406.4(A)–(C))
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4 sets the baseline before the replacement details in 406.4(D). Receptacles must be of the grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, must match the circuit's rating and configuration, and replacements follow a ladder: grounding-type for grounding-type where an EGC exists; where no grounding means exists, the permitted paths are a nongrounding replacement, a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked the same way. The markings are part of the rule, not paperwork. where an EGC exists or is connected under 250.130(C), the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle (406.4(D)(1)). Third replacement option, exactly: a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI, marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground' (406.4(D)(2)(c)).

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.4: Food court and transit waiting-area floor receptacles now need GFCI, a CO/ALR replacement on aluminum wire can skip tamper-resistant, and a replacement must provide GFPE wherever GFPE is now required. GFCI now covers 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp floor receptacles in food courts and airport, bus and train waiting areas that allow food or drink (406.4(G)(2)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Old two-wire house work: carry GFCI receptacles and 'No Equipment Ground' stickers on the truck. An unmarked GFCI swap in a no-ground box fails the detail even though the device itself works.

sections.title: Replacing a receptacle — the replacement must meet today's rules for that location
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4(D) governs what you must do when you swap out an existing receptacle. Where current code requires GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant, or weather-resistant protection at that location, the replacement has to provide it. Where there is no equipment grounding conductor in the box, the permitted paths are a non-grounding-type replacement, a GFCI-type replacement marked as having no equipment ground, or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI device and marked accordingly. You may not simply install a standard grounding receptacle on an ungrounded circuit and leave it looking grounded.

• 406.4(D)(3): Substantiation was provided to that will require ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) receptacles to be listed per 406.4(D)(3).
• 406.4(D)(8): Substantiation has been provided to to require ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) to be provided for replacement receptacles that require GFPE protection by current Code requirements elsewhere in the NEC
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a service swap, test for a real ground first, then pick the replacement path and apply the required marking sticker or engraving before you leave. Photograph the marking for the job record when it is a no-equipment-ground installation.

sections.title: Receptacle assemblies in countertops and work surfaces — listed for the surface
sections.plain_explanation: A receptacle assembly installed in a countertop surface has to be listed for countertop applications — an ordinary receptacle in a cut-in box does not become countertop equipment by being set into the surface. Where the assembly is required to provide GFCI protection under 210.8, it is permitted to be a GFCI receptacle assembly listed for countertop applications. Section 406.5(F) applies the same listing rule to receptacle assemblies in work surfaces. Whether a receptacle may sit face-up in that surface at all is the next rule, 406.5(G).
sections.on_the_job: On a kitchen or bath counter, put the listed pop-up or countertop assembly on the material list — do not plan on a standard duplex in the surface. If that location needs GFCI, order the listed GFCI countertop version of the assembly.
sections.figure_idea: Section through a kitchen island: a listed pop-up countertop assembly with its listing tag called out, beside a standard duplex in a cut box with a red X.

sections.title: Face-up receptacles in countertops — the prohibition is 406.5(G)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 406.5(G) carries the face-up rule for receptacles in counters and work surfaces. Under (G)(1), a receptacle may not be installed in a face-up position in or on a countertop or work surface unless it is listed for countertop or work surface applications. Under (G)(2), a receptacle may not be installed face-up in the area below a sink at all — the listed-assembly exception does not apply there. The hazard is the position itself: a face-up device collects spills, crumbs, and liquids directly into its face. The separate listing rule for receptacle assemblies made for these surfaces is at 406.5(E) and (F), covered on the previous page.
sections.on_the_job: Do not cut a standard duplex into a countertop face-up. Put the receptacle on the side of the cabinet or on the wall at the backsplash, or use a listed pop-up assembly made for countertop use — a listed assembly is the one face-up exception 406.5(G)(1) allows. Nothing goes face-up in the area below a sink.
sections.figure_idea: Countertop from above: a standard duplex crossed out face-up in the surface, a listed pop-up assembly beside it, and the zone below the sink marked no face-up.

sections.title: Receptacles in damp locations
sections.plain_explanation: Section 406.9(A) covers receptacles in damp locations — places that are protected from direct weather but can be damp, such as a covered porch or a carport. The receptacle must be weather-resistant type, and the enclosure must keep moisture out of the wiring connections when no plug is inserted; a cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out is the usual way this is met. Damp is the middle category: not dry indoors, not taking direct rain.
sections.on_the_job: Look up before you decide: if the device can get rained on with the cover open or closed, treat it as wet, not damp, and use the 406.9(B) in-use arrangement. When in doubt, install the wet-location setup — it satisfies the damp case too.

sections.title: Receptacles in wet locations — in-use covers and weather-resistant devices
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(B) covers receptacles in wet locations, where water can reach the device whether or not something is plugged in. The enclosure must stay weatherproof while a plug is inserted and the cord is in use — the bubble or in-use cover — and 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles in wet locations must be weather-resistant (WR) type. An unattended wet-location receptacle, such as one on a house exterior, needs that in-use protection; the rule has specific treatment for receptacles that are attended while in use.

Two details decide inspections here. First, the in-use cover (the outlet box hood) for a wet-location receptacle must be listed and identified as extra duty — the heavier hinged cover — where 406.9(B)(1) requires it; a light flip lid is a damp-location part, not a wet-location one. Second, the weather-resistant requirement in this section reaches the 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles a house and a light commercial job actually use; larger pin-and-sleeve and locking devices follow their own listing for the location.
sections.on_the_job: Stock both parts on the truck: a WR receptacle and an extra-duty in-use cover. A flat flip lid on an exterior receptacle that runs a pump, a charger, or landscape equipment is a correction waiting to happen. Seat the cover gasket fully and route the cord out the bottom notch so the cover can close.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: afternoon rain and irrigation spray make most Florida exterior receptacles wet locations in practice, whatever the plan calls them. Default to WR + in-use cover outside.

sections.title: No receptacles inside the tub or shower zone
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(C) keeps receptacles out of the zone directly inside and immediately around a bathtub or shower stall. In the 2020 arrangement this zone is measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or the shower stall threshold, and no receptacle may be installed within that zone. The rule exists because a person in water is in the worst possible position to contact a device or a cord connected to it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.9(C): Clarified receptacle restrictions in and around bathtubs and showers in Section 406.9(C). A new Exception #4 was added to allow single receptacles within 36" of the tub or shower with limitations.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On layout, mark the zone on the floor plan before you place bath receptacles, not at trim. Vanity receptacles belong outside the zone even when the counter runs close to the tub. If the only wall space is inside the zone, move the discussion to the builder before rough-in, not to the inspector at final.

nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 406.9(C) Bathtub and Shower Space

sections.title: Tamper-resistant receptacles in dwellings and other listed occupancies
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units and in a list of other occupancies where children are present, such as guest rooms, childcare and preschool areas, dormitories, and certain medical and office waiting areas. A TR receptacle has internal shutters that only open when both blades of a plug go in together, so a key or paperclip pushed into one slot does not reach a live contact. The requirement applies at the receptacle locations the article covers, generally those at normal reachable height rather than the listed exceptions such as receptacles high above the floor or inside a luminaire.

The exceptions matter on service work. The TR requirement does not reach:
• Receptacles located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor
• Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or an appliance
• A single receptacle for one appliance, or a duplex for two, in the dedicated space for an appliance that is not easily moved in normal use
• Nongrounding-type replacements installed under 406.4(D) where the box has no grounding means
Everything else at normal device height in the occupancies this section lists is TR — when in doubt, the TR device is the answer.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.12: The tamper-resistant (TR) list grew to ten location groups, adding boathouses, fitness centers, group homes, rehab facilities, nursing homes, foster care, psychiatric hospitals and farm buildings open to the public. Item (1) now lists boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes by name, along with dwelling units and their garages, outbuildings and common areas.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Use TR devices as the default dwelling device and check the exception before you substitute a standard one. A failed shutter on a damaged TR receptacle means replacement, not a standard-device swap (see 406.4(D)).
sections.sharma_note: S-07 pairs with this page: the standard Sharma dwelling device is a TR receptacle, with GFCI/AFCI protection supplied by the DFN breaker rather than by a GFCI receptacle.

sections.title: Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 408 covers the boards themselves: switchboards, switchgear, and the panelboards Sharma installs on nearly every job. For residential and light commercial work the live parts of this article are the circuit directory, identification of circuits, closing unused openings, overcurrent protection of the panelboard, and the rule that breakers be the type listed for the panel they sit in. The industrial switchboard sections matter on larger commercial gear; the directory and listing rules matter everywhere.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.38: The enclosure rule now ties to fault current: once available fault current passes 10,000 amps, the panelboard and its enclosure have to be evaluated as a matched combination. If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination.
• 408.9: Two paths for a replacement panelboard in an existing enclosure: listed for that enclosure keeps its rating; if not, it's identified for the use up to 10,000 amps available fault current, field labeled above. Listed for that specific enclosure, by catalog number or dimensions? The replacement keeps its short-circuit current rating (408.9(A)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Treat the panel as a document, not just a box: directory filled in, circuits identified at every disconnect, unused openings closed, and only listed breakers installed. An inspector can fail a beautiful rough-in on a blank directory.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: all new Sharma gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, install Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space.

If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination.

sections.title: The circuit directory — specific, on site, and kept current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(A) requires every circuit and circuit modification to be identified at the panelboard with enough detail to tell circuits apart, and a circuit directory (or circuit identification) must be provided at the board. Generic labels like 'plugs,' 'lights,' or 'bedroom' written for a different house do not meet the intent; the identification has to describe the actual purpose or use of each circuit in that building. Spare positions must be marked as spares, and the directory must be updated when circuits change.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.4(A): Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Fill the directory at trim, from the actual panel schedule, and have the person who wired the house check it circuit by circuit with a tester or by switching. A directory copied from the plan without field verification is how 'Kitchen' ends up feeding the water heater.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the directory is part of the finished product the builder sees. Neat, specific, and correct — 'NE bedroom receptacles,' not 'BR.'

Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.4 Circuit directory and source labels

sections.title: Identification of the source of supply
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(B) addresses panelboards supplied by a feeder: the board must be marked to identify where its supply comes from when that source is in a different location or is not obvious, so that a person standing at the panel can find the disconnect that kills it. Companion identification rules in Article 408 also require disconnects and circuits to be marked for their purpose where they are not self-evident. The theme of the whole part is that nobody should have to guess what feeds what.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.4: Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a sub-panel, label the feeder source (for example, 'Fed from Main Panel, Garage') at the sub-panel and label the feeder breaker at the source panel. Do the same for any panel fed from a generator or a second service, and make the two labels agree with each other.

In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.4 Circuit directory and source labels

sections.title: The equipment's short-circuit current rating must cover the available fault current
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.6 requires switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where they are installed. A panel that matches the job on volts and amps can still be the wrong panel if its SCCR is below the fault current the service can deliver into a short. This requirement was added in the 2020 edition, which is why older change-out habits never asked the question.
sections.on_the_job: On a service change or a commercial panel set, get the available fault current (from the utility or the design documents) and compare it with the SCCR marked on the gear before the gear is ordered. Record both numbers in the job file. If the fault current is unknown, that is an engineering question for Mike, not a field estimate.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 pairs with this page: new Sharma gear is Siemens, and the SCCR check is part of selecting it, not an afterthought at inspection.

sections.title: Unused openings must be closed
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.7 requires unused openings in a panelboard (and in switchboards and switchgear) to be closed with closures that give protection substantially equal to the wall of the enclosure. An open breaker space with a missing filler plate is an exposed live-part opening, a dust and vermin path, and an automatic correction. Tape is not a closure.
sections.on_the_job: Keep listed filler plates for the panel brand on the trim truck. Before final, open every panel, run a finger check for open spaces, blank plates, and missing knock-out closures, and close them with the manufacturer's part.
sections.sharma_note: S-02/S-03 apply to the closure as well: use the filler listed for that panel, not a near-fit from another brand.

sections.title: The panelboard itself must be protected
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.36 requires a panelboard to be protected by an overcurrent device rated no higher than the panelboard's rating, located in or ahead of the board, with listed exceptions such as certain existing installations and mains supplied under specific service rules. In plain terms, a 100A panel may not sit behind a 200A breaker just because the feeder wires are large. The bus has its own limit and something must enforce it.
sections.on_the_job: When you set a sub-panel, check three numbers together: panel bus rating, feeder conductor ampacity, and the breaker feeding it. The smallest applicable limit governs. Record all three on the panel schedule for the office file.

sections.title: Each grounded (neutral) conductor gets its own terminal
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in a panelboard to terminate in its own individual terminal that is not used for any other conductor, unless the terminal is specifically identified for more than one. Doubling two neutrals under one screw is a classic correction: when one circuit is worked on, loosening the shared terminal can open the neutral of a live circuit sharing it. Equipment grounding conductors follow their own termination rules and the panel's listing; the one-per-terminal discipline on this page is about the grounded conductors.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, land neutrals one to a screw and torque them; never park a second neutral under a screw 'temporarily.' On a panel change-out, budget the time to separate doubled neutrals — finding them is part of the job, and the directory update in 408.4(A) happens on the same visit.

sections.title: A panelboard may not be installed face-up
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.43 prohibits installing a panelboard in a face-up position. A load center belongs on a vertical surface with its breakers oriented as the listing intends; a face-up board collects debris and water, and its breakers do not operate or indicate as designed. The rule was added in the 2020 edition and most often matters on custom commercial millwork and unusual equipment layouts, not on a standard house panel.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.43: Panelboards can't be installed facing down now. Added to the 2020 face-up ban, a panelboard's front can point neither at the ceiling nor at the floor. A panelboard can't be mounted face-down, with its front pointing at the floor, such as on the underside of a ceiling or platform.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: If a plan or a cabinet detail shows a panel lying flat, stop at rough-in and raise it with the builder — the fix is a layout change, not a field workaround. Check orientation on any pre-built equipment package before it is set.

sections.title: Industrial control panels — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 409 covers industrial control panels: the factory- or field-assembled panels that control industrial machinery, with their short-circuit current rating (SCCR) marking, supply conductor sizing, and internal wiring rules. The SCCR is the headline item — a panel may not be installed where the available fault current exceeds the rating marked on it. Sharma meets this article on light commercial and equipment work rather than in houses.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 409.60: Section 409.60 for industrial control panels was restructured, creating (A) Grounding and (B) Bonding.
• 409.70: New Section 409.70 has been added requiring surge protection for industrial control panels.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the SCCR on the panel label and compare it with the available fault current at its supply before you set the panel. If the panel has no SCCR marking or the fault current is unknown, stop and take it to Mike — that is an engineering check, not a field guess.

sections.title: Industrial control panels — marking and short-circuit current rating (409.110)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 409 panels — the factory-built control panels that run machinery and HVAC equipment — must be marked under 409.110 with the panel's electrical ratings, and the marking includes the panel's short-circuit current rating (SCCR). The SCCR is a ceiling: the panel may not be installed where the available fault current exceeds it. Read the panel label the way you read a motor nameplate before the panel is set — supply voltage, phases, and SCCR all come off that mark, and a missing or illegible SCCR is a stop-and-ask, not a guess.
sections.on_the_job: On light-commercial equipment swaps, photograph the control panel label with the rest of the nameplates. If the new panel's SCCR is lower than what the service can deliver, that is an engineering conversation before the panel is set, not after.
sections.figure_idea: Sample panel label with the SCCR line circled next to voltage and phase.

sections.title: Luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 410 covers light fixtures in the broad code sense: luminaires, lampholders, and lamps, including where they may be installed, how they are supported, temperature limits near combustible material, and the special zones in bathtubs, showers, and clothes closets. The two pages Sharma hits constantly are the tub/shower zone and the closet rules. Fixture listing and its instructions (110.3(B)) do half the work in this article — the box and the spec sheet are part of the code answer.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 410.184: Cord-connected grow lights on circuits over 150 volts to ground, like 277 volts, now need a listed special-purpose GFCI (SPGFCI). The rule also now spells out which cords trigger it. Grow lights on a circuit over 150 volts to ground, such as 277 volts from a 480Y/277 system, must be protected by a listed SPGFCI.
• 410.71: LED fixtures with double-ended (tube-style) lamps and drivers serviceable in place now need the same disconnect fluorescent fixtures already needed. The rule moved from 410.130(G) to 410.71. Indoors outside dwellings, a disconnect is now required on LED luminaires that use double-ended lamps and have field-serviceable drivers (410.71(1)).
• 410.2: Determined that ballasts, LED drivers, and lamps should be added into updated Section 410.2 for items not allowed to be reconditioned.
• Article 410: A new Part XVII was added to Article 410 to address the increasing use of germicidal luminaires for disinfecting purposes. These products are increasingly being used due to the COVID 19 pandemic and other concerns.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the fixture's own listing before you rough the box: weight, temperature rating, damp/wet rating, and closet or shower suitability are all on the label or the cut sheet, not in the field manual.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma bath practice (company practice, not 410): vanity lighting plus the architect's wet-location shower light, with no extra general ceiling light added by habit. Follow the plan; do not add or delete bath lights on your own.

sections.title: Luminaires in the bathtub and shower zone
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.10(D) controls fixtures inside the zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside that zone a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where it is subject to shower spray, and certain fixture types — including hanging fixtures, pendants, and ceiling-suspended fans — are not permitted in the zone at all. A fixture outside the zone is not governed by this subsection even if it is in the same bathroom.
sections.on_the_job: Mark the zone on the plan at rough-in and check every bath fixture against it, including the shower light and any fan/light combo. Confirm the damp or wet marking on the fixture label matches where it actually sits, and keep the label information in the job file.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the architect's specified shower light is the fixture of record — install the listed wet-location model specified, not a damp-only substitute from stock.

sections.title: Luminaires in clothes closets — permitted types and clearances
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.16 controls what may light a clothes closet and how far it must sit from the closet storage space — the volume defined in 410.2: 24 inches out from the side and back walls, from the floor up to 6 feet or the highest clothes-hanging rod, and 12 inches out from the walls, or the width of the shelf if greater, from there up to the ceiling. Permitted types [410.16(A)]: surface-mounted or recessed incandescent or LED luminaires with a completely enclosed light source; surface-mounted or recessed fluorescent luminaires; and surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaires identified as suitable for installation within the closet storage space. Not permitted [410.16(B)]: incandescent luminaires with open or partially enclosed lamps, and pendant luminaires or lampholders. Minimum clearances from the nearest point of the storage space [410.16(C)]: 12 inches for a surface-mounted incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source, installed on the ceiling or the wall above the door; 6 inches for a surface-mounted fluorescent luminaire in the same positions; 6 inches for a recessed incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source; and 6 inches for a recessed fluorescent luminaire. A surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaire identified for use within the closet storage space may be installed inside the storage space itself [410.16(C)(5)].
sections.on_the_job: Measure the clearance from the storage space, not from the wall or the clothes — that 24-inch and 12-inch volume exists on paper even in an empty closet. Default habit: an enclosed LED fixture, surface-mounted at 12 inches clear of the storage space or recessed at 6 inches, and never a pendant or an exposed lamp in a closet.

sections.title: Recessed luminaires — insulation contact and thermal protection
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.116 covers recessed luminaires: the clearance they must keep from combustible material, the thermal protection that shuts the fixture down if it overheats, and the difference between fixtures listed for direct contact with insulation (Type IC) and those that must keep insulation away. An IC rating is a property of the specific fixture, not of recessed fixtures in general. The fixture's marking also decides whether it may be installed in a ceiling that will be insulated after the fact.
sections.on_the_job: Read the housing label before the ceiling closes: IC or non-IC, and the insulation clearance if it is non-IC. In an insulated Florida attic ceiling, a non-IC can buried in blown insulation is both a code correction and a heat problem — flag it at rough-in, while the fix is still cheap.

sections.title: Lighting systems operating at 30 volts or less — article intro
sections.plain_explanation: Article 411 covers low-voltage lighting systems operating at 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC or less — and only 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC where contact with water is likely: the listed system, its power supply, and the secondary wiring that feeds the fixtures. These systems are installed as a listed assembly, not assembled from loose parts in the field, and the secondary conductors have their own rules distinct from ordinary branch wiring. Sharma meets this article mainly in landscape-style and specialty accent lighting inside a project.
sections.on_the_job: Install the system as the listed package: listed power supply, listed fixtures, and the manufacturer's wiring instructions. Do not extend a 30V secondary with branch-circuit wire methods or bury connections the listing does not allow.

sections.title: Low-voltage lighting systems — where they may and may not go (Article 411)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at not more than 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC (411.1, 2020) — the listed low-voltage systems behind a lot of LED tape, under-cabinet, and accent work. The system must be listed as a complete system or assembled from listed parts, the power source limits the secondary circuit (the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes), and the bare-conductor versions carry location limits: not concealed or run through walls, floors, or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it, and kept clear of pools, spas, and similar locations except as the article allows. A loose power supply and a roll of tape bought online is not an Article 411 system. Location limits are 411.5: not concealed or extended through a building wall, floor or ceiling unless wired with a Chapter 3 method or Class 2 wiring where the power supply is Class 2, and not within 10 ft of pools, spas, fountains or similar locations unless Article 680 permits. 411.4 itself is the listing rule (a complete listed system, or assembled from listed parts).
sections.on_the_job: Spec the listed system — power supply, cable, and fixtures from one listed family — and keep the driver accessible. Inspectors ask whose system it is; 'the homeowner bought it online' is not an answer.
sections.figure_idea: System diagram: listed power unit to secondary cable to fixtures, with the 30 V and 25 A limits marked on the secondary side.

sections.title: Appliances — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 422 covers appliances: water heaters, dishwashers, disposals, ranges and cooktops, dryers as appliances, space heaters that plug or hard-wire as appliances, and similar equipment. Its working parts are branch-circuit sizing for specific appliances, permitted cord-and-plug connections, overcurrent protection, and the disconnecting means that lets a servicer kill the appliance safely. Where an appliance is also a motor load or also HVAC equipment, Articles 430 and 440 may govern instead or in addition — check the appliance's own article first.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 422.16: Dishwasher and trash compactor cords now follow matching rules, and a smoothed edge is named as acceptable protection where a cord passes through a cabinet opening. Trash compactor cords now get the same protection dishwasher cords already had where they pass through a cabinet wall.
• 422.18: A new 422.18(B) keeps metal paddle fan parts out of the 3 ft by 8 ft zone around a tub or shower, and fan support now uses the new WSCR terms. New 422.18(B) bars metal paddle fan parts from the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up from a tub's rim or a shower's threshold.
• Article 422: Sections 422.3, 422.4, 422.15, 422.23, 422.46. 422.50 for appliances were deleted from the 2023 edition of the NEC.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: For every appliance on a job, settle three things from the nameplate before rough-in is closed: circuit size, cord-and-plug or hard-wired, and where the disconnect will be. The nameplate, not the catalog photo, is the source.
sections.sharma_note: S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit and is not lumped onto a circuit shared with the hood or anything else. The wire (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA) is not settled until Mike Holt rules.

Trash compactor cords now get the same protection dishwasher cords already had where they pass through a cabinet wall.

sections.title: GFCI protection required for specific appliances
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.5 names the appliances that must have Class A GFCI protection for personnel wherever they are installed — the duty travels with the appliance, on top of the room rules in 210.8, and meeting one does not erase the other. The 2020 list at 422.5(A) is: automotive vacuum machines; drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations; cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washing machines; tire inflation machines; vending machines; sump pumps; and dishwashers. It reaches appliances rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single- or 3-phase, cord-and-plug-connected or hardwired, and 210.8(D) points to this same list. The protection must be readily accessible and provided by one of the methods 422.5(B) permits — a GFCI breaker, a GFCI receptacle, or another listed point the section allows. Edition caution: wider appliance lists circulating from NEC 2023 research are not the 2020 list — in 2020, ranges, dryers, and microwaves pick up their GFCI duties through the location rules in 210.8, not through 422.5. NEC 2020 removed the 'provided for public use' condition and added sump pumps. 422.5(B) locations: the branch-circuit overcurrent device; a device or outlet within the supply circuit; an integral part of the attachment plug; within the supply cord not more than 12 in. from the attachment plug; or factory-installed within the appliance.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 422.5 / 210.8(D): 2023 210.8(D) adds electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens to the appliances needing GFCI, correlated with the 422.5(A) list.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Check an appliance against both lists: 210.8 for the room and receptacle, and 422.5 for the appliance itself. On Sharma work the DFN breaker usually supplies this protection for a 120V appliance circuit (S-07); confirm the breaker type actually provides GFCI, not AFCI only.

sections.title: Branch circuits for appliances (422.10)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.10 starts appliance work with the circuit: the branch circuit must be sized for the appliance it serves, using the appliance's marked rating, and an individual branch circuit — one that supplies only that appliance — is the default pattern for the big fixed appliances. Where two or more appliances share a circuit, this section's load rules and the general rules of Articles 210 and 220 both apply. When the nameplate and the circuit disagree, the circuit gets corrected; the appliance does not get derated by hope.
sections.on_the_job: Takeoff habit: every fixed appliance on the plans gets a line — appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect. If a plan shows the appliance but no circuit home, that is an open question for the packet, not a field surprise.
sections.figure_idea: Takeoff worksheet strip: appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect — four boxes in a row.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for appliances (422.11)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.11 protects the appliance at the size the appliance was built for. Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, that marking governs. For a single non-motor appliance fastened in place and rated over 13.3 amperes, where the appliance is not marked with a maximum OCPD: 20A maximum if the appliance is rated 13.3A or less; 150% of the rated current maximum if rated over 13.3A, and where 150% does not land on a standard rating the next higher standard size is permitted (422.11(E)). — a ceiling, not a target. Motor-operated appliances follow the motor rules for their protection, and infrared heating appliances carry their own subdivision limits in this section. 422.11(F): resistance-type heating elements in electric heating appliances rated over 48A must be subdivided, each subdivided load not over 48A and protected at not more than 60A.
sections.on_the_job: Read the appliance label before the breaker is chosen, every time. 'It matched the panel schedule from the last job' is how a 50 A device lands on an appliance marked 30 A maximum.
sections.figure_idea: Appliance label zoom: 'MAX FUSE / BREAKER 30 A' with an arrow to the panel breaker slot.

sections.title: Storage water heaters — treat the load as continuous for circuit sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.13 sizes the branch circuit for a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less at not less than 125 percent of the heater's nameplate rating. In practice that is why a common 4500W, 240V heater (18.75A) lands on a 25A minimum calculation and is conventionally wired on a 30A circuit with 10 AWG copper — the arithmetic must be run for the actual nameplate on the actual job, not copied from the last house. The heater is treated this way because it can run for long stretches recovering a tank.
sections.on_the_job:
Do the division every time: nameplate watts divided by voltage, times 1.25, then choose the standard breaker and conductor that cover it. Write the result on the panel schedule so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer it.

Worked example: a 5,500 W, 240 V heater draws 5,500 ÷ 240 = 22.9 A; × 1.25 = 28.6 A minimum circuit — a 30A breaker on 10 AWG copper covers it. The standard 4,500 W heater works out to 18.75 A × 1.25 = 23.4 A, which is why it also lands on the same 30A / 10 AWG circuit.

sections.title: Cord-and-plug connection for range hoods
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.16(B)(4) is the provision the brief assigns to cord-and-plug-connected range hoods: a listed range hood may be connected with a cord and plug where the conditions of that subsection are met, including that the hood is marked for that connection method and the receptacle arrangement matches the rule. Cord connection is what lets the hood be removed for service without unwiring it, but it is only permitted because the appliance and the installation meet the listed conditions — not as a general shortcut for any fixed appliance.
sections.on_the_job: Confirm the hood's instructions allow cord connection and that the receptacle location matches the plan before rough-in. If the hood is listed for hard-wiring only, hard-wire it; the cord kit in the truck does not override the listing.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note (company practice, not a 422 rule): the range hood often rides the dishwasher/disposal circuit in Sharma design practice. S-06 still stands on its own — the microwave keeps its own dedicated 20A circuit and is never lumped in with the hood. The wire size on that circuit is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).

sections.title: Disconnecting means for permanently connected appliances
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.31 covers how a permanently connected appliance is disconnected for service. Depending on the appliance's rating, the disconnect may be a switch or breaker that meets the article's conditions, and for larger appliances the disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position or meet the subsection that applies to its size. The intent is simple: the person servicing the appliance must be able to cut its power and keep it cut. The branch-circuit breaker can serve this role only where the conditions for doing so are met.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, decide where each hard-wired appliance's disconnect lives and confirm a servicer can reach it. A water heater, an air handler, or a cooktop whose only disconnect is an unlabelled breaker two rooms away is a conversation to have before final, not after.

sections.title: Fixed electric space-heating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 424 covers heating that is built into the building: baseboard heaters, wall heaters, radiant panels and cables, duct heaters, and boilers used for space heat. Its core ideas are that heating loads are treated as continuous, that the equipment must be listed and installed to its instructions, and that disconnects and controls must let the heater be serviced and shut off safely. In Florida houses Sharma meets this article most often at duct heat strips in an air handler and at the occasional wall or bath heater.

sections.title: Branch circuits for fixed electric space heating (424.4(A), 424.4(B))
sections.plain_explanation: Fixed electric space heating — baseboard, wall heaters, ceiling heat, and the electric heat built into equipment — is served by individual branch circuits under 424.4(A), with the central systems the article names as the exception pattern. Under 424.4(B) the heating load is treated as continuous: branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit, before any other load is considered. A heater is not a convenience load that happens to get warm; it runs for hours at full draw. Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30A; in other than dwelling units, fixed infrared heating may be on circuits up to 50A (424.4(A)). (424.3(A)/(B) are the 2017 numbers.)
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 4,800 W, 240 V wall heater draws 20 A. Continuous sizing makes the circuit 20 × 1.25 = 25 A — so the circuit is built at 25 A or above, never the 20 A circuit the raw math suggests.
sections.figure_idea: One heater, two math lines: nameplate amps, then the 125 percent continuous line landing on the breaker size.

sections.title: Branch-circuit sizing for fixed space heat — 125 percent
sections.plain_explanation: Section 424.4(B) is where this rule lives in the 2020 edition — it was 424.3(B) in 2017, before the Article 424 reorganization. The 2020 text states the sizing directly instead of using the old 'shall be considered continuous load' sentence: the branch-circuit conductors for fixed electric space-heating equipment and any associated motors shall be sized not smaller than 125 percent of the load. Overcurrent protection is sized at the same 125 percent through the continuous-load rules of 210.19(A)(1) and 210.20(A), so in practice both the conductors and the breaker come out at 125 percent of the total load connected to the circuit, heater plus any blower or fan motor in the same equipment.
sections.on_the_job:
Run the math at 125 percent: total nameplate amps, heater plus motor, times 1.25 — then select the conductor and the breaker.

Worked example: a 10 kW duct heater at 240 V draws 41.7 A; × 1.25 = 52.1 A — conductors rated at least 52.1 A (6 AWG copper at the 75°C column gives 65 A) on a 60A breaker, and the blower motor amps in the same equipment are added to the heater amps before the 125 percent is applied.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Section 424.19 requires a disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment that disconnects the heater and its controller, placed so the equipment can be serviced safely, with provisions for locking or for the breaker arrangement depending on the installation. A duct heater inside an air handler is normally disconnected at the air handler's disconnect, which is why the 440/424 boundary matters on an HVAC change-out: the heat strips and the blower are one piece of equipment at service time.
sections.on_the_job: Confirm the disconnect kills the strips and the blower together, and that it is within reach of the person servicing the unit. On a change-out, if you move the disconnect, re-verify the heat-strip circuit at the new location before start-up.

sections.title: Motors, motor circuits, and controllers — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 430 is the longest working article in Chapter 4 and the one most often misapplied, because it is a system, not a single rule: conductors sized from table full-load current, separate overload protection sized from the nameplate, short-circuit and ground-fault protection sized from its own tables and percentages, a controller, and a disconnect within sight. Each of those five jobs has its own sizing basis, and using one number for all five is the classic 430 error. Air-conditioning equipment is pulled out of parts of 430 by Article 440, which has its own nameplate-driven rules — always check which article governs the equipment in front of you.

sections.title: Which current do you size from — table values vs. nameplate
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.6 is the traffic rule for the whole article. For sizing conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit/ground-fault protection, you use the full-load current values from the Article 430 tables for the motor's horsepower and voltage — not the amps printed on that particular motor's nameplate, because the next replacement motor may differ. Overload protection is the exception: it is sized from the actual nameplate current of the motor installed, because it protects that specific machine. Mixing those two bases up is the single most common motor calculation error.

Table values the crews use most — single-phase from Table 430.248, three-phase from Table 430.250:
• 1/2 hp, 115 V — 9.8 A
• 1 hp, 115 V — 16 A
• 1 hp, 230 V — 8 A
• 2 hp, 230 V — 12 A
• 3 hp, 230 V — 17 A
• 5 hp, 230 V — 28 A
• 1 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 4.6 A
• 5 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 16.7 A
• 10 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 30.8 A
• 10 hp, 460 V, 3-phase — 14 A
The fuller table is on the 430.250 page. If the horsepower and voltage in front of you are not listed here, pull the value from the printed table for that combination — do not scale from a nearby row.
sections.on_the_job: Keep two numbers on your worksheet and label them: 'Table FLC' and 'Nameplate FLA.' If a number on your page is not labelled, stop and label it before you size anything from it.

sections.title: Conductors for a single motor — 125 percent of table full-load current
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.22 sizes the branch-circuit conductors feeding one continuous-duty motor at not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables. The extra quarter covers the heating of a motor that runs for long periods at full load. Intermittent and short-time duty motors are treated under their own parts of this section, so the duty rating on the nameplate decides which rule you are in before you do any arithmetic.
sections.on_the_job:
Take the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage, multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the correct temperature column for the terminations. Do not size the wire from the nameplate amps and do not round the 125 percent away.

Worked example: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table FLC of 28 A (Table 430.248). Conductors: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A minimum — 10 AWG copper at the 75°C column (35 A) is the smallest conductor that covers it, before any voltage-drop or adjustment checks.

sections.title: Conductors feeding several motors
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.24 sizes conductors that feed two or more motors (or motors with other loads): take 125 percent of the full-load current of the largest motor, add the full-load currents of the other motors at 100 percent, and add any other loads under their own rules, all using the Article 430 table values. The largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the rest are added at face value, on the reasonable basis that the feeder sees the sum. It is the feeder-level companion to the single-motor rule in 430.22.
sections.on_the_job: Build the sum in a labelled column — largest motor first at 125 percent, then each additional motor at 100 percent — so the next person can audit it. Do not apply 125 percent to every motor on the feeder, and do not size a multi-motor feeder from one nameplate.

sections.title: Overload protection — protects the motor from running too hot
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.32 requires overload protection for continuous-duty motors over the small sizes the article sets, sized from the motor's nameplate full-load current with the percentage depending on the motor's service factor and temperature-rise markings. The overload device watches running current over time and trips before the windings cook; it is not there to clear a short circuit, which is the branch protective device's job. A motor with built-in thermal protection meets this requirement through its own device where the article allows it.

The percentages in 430.32(A)(1), applied to the nameplate full-load current:
• Motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater — 125 percent
• Motor with a marked temperature rise of 40°C or less — 125 percent
• All other motors — 115 percent
If an overload selected at those percentages will not let the motor start or carry its load, 430.32(C) permits stepping up — to not more than 140 percent for the first two cases, 130 percent for all others. The step-up is a documented exception for a motor that will not run, not the starting point for selection.
sections.on_the_job: Read service factor and rise off the nameplate before you select or set an overload. If the overload trips repeatedly, measure the running amps and find the mechanical cause — do not solve a tripping overload by setting it higher than 430.32 permits.

sections.title: Branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for motors
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.52 sizes the device that clears a fault on a motor branch circuit, using the percentages in Table 430.52 applied to the table full-load current, with the device type (fuses, inverse-time breaker, instantaneous-trip breaker, and so on) deciding which column applies. These percentages are deliberately far above running current, because the device must ride through motor starting inrush without opening, while still clearing a fault. That is why a motor circuit can legally have a breaker that looks oversized for its wire — the overload device, not the breaker, is protecting the motor and, through its sizing rules, the circuit against overload.

Table 430.52 maximum ratings, as a percentage of table full-load current:
• Nontime-delay (single-element) fuses — 300 percent
• Dual-element (time-delay) fuses — 175 percent
• Inverse-time circuit breakers — 250 percent
• Instantaneous-trip breakers — 800 percent, with the table's notes permitting up to 1300 percent for the listed motor designs and sizes
Worked example: the 5 hp, 230 V motor at 28 A table FLC takes an inverse-time breaker of at most 28 × 2.50 = 70 A. If that device will not hold through starting, 430.52(C)(1) Exception 1 permits an inverse-time breaker up to 400 percent where the FLC is 100 A or less — an exception to document, not a habit.
sections.on_the_job: Never judge a motor circuit by house-circuit instincts. Check all three together: conductor at 125 percent of table FLC (430.22), overload from the nameplate (430.32), fault protection from Table 430.52. If one of the three is missing from the job paperwork, the calculation is not finished.
