sections.title: Feeder protection where several motors share a feeder (430.62)
sections.plain_explanation: When one feeder supplies several motor branch circuits, 430.62(A) caps the feeder's protective device: no larger than the largest branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault device on the feeder, plus the full-load currents of the other motors on that feeder. The feeder conductors themselves are sized under 430.24 — 125 percent of the largest motor plus 100 percent of the rest. The two rules work as a pair: the wire math keeps the feeder from running hot, and the device math keeps a fault on one motor from being invisible to a feeder breaker sized for everything at once.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: three motors at 14 A, 10 A, and 10 A table FLC, largest branch device 40 A. Feeder device ceiling: 40 + 10 + 10 = 60 A. Feeder conductors: 14 × 1.25 + 10 + 10 = 37.5 A minimum ampacity before other adjustments.
sections.figure_idea: Feeder tree: three motor branches joining one feeder, the two formulas written on the feeder segment.

sections.title: The motor disconnect must be within sight
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.102 places the disconnecting means for a motor and its controller within sight from the equipment it disconnects — visible and not more than 50 ft away, the Article 100 meaning of 'in sight.' The person servicing the machine must be able to see the disconnect, or the disconnect must be of a type that can be locked open under the conditions the article allows. A breaker in a panel across the building, with no lockable arrangement, does not give a servicer control of the machine in front of them.
sections.on_the_job: Stand at the motor and point at its disconnect before you call the job done. If you cannot see it, either move it, add the local disconnect, or confirm the lockable arrangement the article permits and document it. The same within-sight habit is what 440.14 demands for HVAC equipment.

sections.title: What may serve as the motor disconnect
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.109 lists the types of switches and devices permitted to serve as a motor disconnect, including horsepower-rated switches and listed circuit breakers, with the permitted type depending on the motor's size and duty. A general-use switch that is fine for a lighting load is not automatically a motor disconnect; the device must be rated for interrupting a motor circuit of that horsepower. Small fractional-horsepower motors have their own permitted arrangements under this section and 430.111.
sections.on_the_job: Read the horsepower rating on the switch, not just the amp rating, before you land a motor on it. When the disconnect is a breaker in a panelboard, confirm it is a permitted type for that motor and that the within-sight rule in 430.102 is separately satisfied.

sections.title: Rating of the motor disconnect — at least 115 percent
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.110 sizes the disconnecting means for a motor circuit: a general-use switch used as a motor disconnect must have an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables, and horsepower-rated devices are selected by their horsepower rating for the motor served. The disconnect is a switching device that must safely make and break motor current, which is why its sizing basis is its own rule and not simply 'match the breaker.' Combined with 430.102 (within sight) and 430.109 (permitted types), this completes the disconnect picture.
sections.on_the_job: Check two markings on a motor disconnect: the amp rating against 115 percent of table FLC, or the horsepower rating against the motor. If either fails, the disconnect is the wrong device even if it has worked for years on the old motor.

sections.title: Conductors to drives and power conversion equipment (430.122)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.122 sizes the conductors feeding adjustable-speed drives and other power conversion equipment from the equipment's rated input current — not from the motor's horsepower table. The circuit conductors must have an ampacity of at least 125 percent of the drive's rated input current, and where the equipment has a bypass or its own rating rules, the section follows the larger demand. A drive can draw more at its input than the motor table suggests, so the drive nameplate — input amps — is the document that sizes this wire.
sections.on_the_job: Swapping a starter for a VFD on a pump or air handler: photograph the drive's input rating before ordering wire. Reusing the old starter's wire size without the input-current check is the standard failure.
sections.figure_idea: Nameplate zoom: 'INPUT 460 V 21 A' feeding the 125 percent math line.

sections.title: Motor full-load current tables — the working values (430.248 / 430.250)
sections.plain_explanation:
Tables 430.248 (single-phase) and 430.250 (three-phase) are the source of the table full-load current used for conductor, disconnect, controller, and short-circuit sizing under 430.6. The combinations below are the ones Sharma's crews meet most; the printed tables govern for anything not listed here.

Single-phase (Table 430.248):
• 1/2 hp — 9.8 A at 115 V, 4.9 A at 230 V
• 1 hp — 16 A at 115 V, 8 A at 230 V
• 1-1/2 hp — 20 A at 115 V, 10 A at 230 V
• 2 hp — 24 A at 115 V, 12 A at 230 V
• 3 hp — 34 A at 115 V, 17 A at 230 V
• 5 hp — 28 A at 230 V
• 7-1/2 hp — 40 A at 230 V
• 10 hp — 50 A at 230 V

Three-phase (Table 430.250):
• 1 hp — 4.6 A at 208 V, 2.1 A at 460 V
• 3 hp — 10.6 A at 208 V, 4.8 A at 460 V
• 5 hp — 16.7 A at 208 V, 7.6 A at 460 V
• 7-1/2 hp — 24.2 A at 208 V, 11 A at 460 V
• 10 hp — 30.8 A at 208 V, 14 A at 460 V
• 15 hp — 46.2 A at 208 V, 21 A at 460 V
• 20 hp — 59.4 A at 208 V, 27 A at 460 V
• 25 hp — 74.8 A at 208 V, 34 A at 460 V
sections.on_the_job: Keep the two bases separate (430.6): these table numbers size the wire, the disconnect, and the fault protection; the overloads still come off the nameplate of the motor actually installed. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC even when its nameplate amps differ from the old motor's.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet card: horsepower down the left, 115 / 208 / 230 / 460 V columns across, the common FLC values filled in — a glovebox version of Tables 430.248 and 430.250.

sections.title: Air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 440 takes hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors and air-conditioning equipment out of the general motor rules and gives them a nameplate-driven system. The equipment nameplate states the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP, sometimes marked MOP or 'max fuse/breaker'), and those two printed numbers — not a horsepower table — size the circuit. Article 440 also sets the disconnect rule Sharma's crews use daily: within sight, readily accessible, at the equipment. Where 430 and 440 disagree for a compressor, 440 governs. Florida settles the common condenser question for houses: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment on one- and two-family dwellings.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 440.11: If unqualified people can readily reach an A/C or refrigeration disconnect, any door or hinged cover that exposes energized parts must take a tool to open or accept a lock. Disconnect readily accessible to unqualified people? A door or hinged cover that opens onto energized parts must need a tool or be lockable.
• 440.8: Section 440.8 now also controls location: A/C and refrigeration equipment can't sit in the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold. Air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment stays out of the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the nameplate before you run the wire, every unit, every change-out. A replacement condenser with a higher MCA than the old one is a new circuit calculation, not a like-for-like swap. Photograph the nameplate for the job file at rough-in and again at start-up.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (tip, not an S-rule): the condenser is wired to the nameplate MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. The 210.8(F) GFCI question for outdoor outlets/equipment has varied by TIA and local amendment — confirm the AHJ position on the job rather than assuming; see the Chapter 2 cross-link on the 440.4(B) page.

Disconnect readily accessible to unqualified people? A door or hinged cover that opens onto energized parts must need a tool or be lockable.

sections.title: Reading the HVAC nameplate — MCA and MOCP do the sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Section 440.4(B) covers the nameplate marking for equipment with a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor: the plate carries the rated-load current and the branch-circuit selection current, and the manufacturer's marked minimum circuit ampacity and maximum overcurrent device rating are built from them. In field language: MCA tells you the smallest conductor ampacity the circuit may have; MOCP tells you the largest fuse or breaker you may protect it with. A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not. The plate, not a tonnage rule of thumb, is the calculation.
sections.on_the_job:
On every condenser and air handler: record MCA, MOCP, voltage, and phase from the plate. Wire to at least MCA, protect at no more than MOCP, and if the installed breaker or wire disagrees with a change-out unit's new plate, stop and tell the office before start-up — that is a change order conversation, not a field improvisation.

Worked example: a condenser plate reads MCA 24.5 A, MOCP 40 A. The conductor ampacity must be at least 24.5 A — 10 AWG copper (35 A at the 75°C column) covers it — and the breaker may be anything up to 40 A; Sharma's standard install protects it at the MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. A same-tonnage change-out plate reading MCA 17.5 / MOCP 30 is a different circuit — the plate, not the tons, decides.
sections.sharma_note: Cross-link (Chapter 2): the question of GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC equipment under 210.8(F) is handled on the Chapter 2 pages and is deliberately not resolved here; local AHJ position governs on the job.

sections.title: Short-circuit current rating of air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Section 440.10 requires motor controllers and industrial control equipment used with air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to have a short-circuit current rating suitable for the available fault current, with the rating marked as the article requires. It is the Article 440 companion to 408.6 and 409: modern packaged HVAC gear and its control panels carry an SCCR, and a unit installed where the available fault current exceeds it is a mismatch even when MCA and MOCP are perfect. The issue arises on commercial rooftops and larger services, rarely on a house condenser.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial HVAC work, add SCCR to the nameplate photograph set: MCA, MOCP, and SCCR, plus the available fault current when the design provides it. A mismatch goes to Mike before the unit is set, not to the inspector at final.

sections.title: Rating the air-conditioning disconnect (440.12)
sections.plain_explanation: The disconnecting means for hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor equipment is rated under 440.12, separately from the branch-circuit protection in 440.22. The disconnect's ampere rating must be at least 115 percent of the nameplate rated-load current or the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater — or the disconnect may be chosen by the horsepower-equivalent method the section allows. A disconnect that matches the breaker size by habit can still be undersized by this section, because the two devices answer different questions.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: nameplate rated-load current 28 A. Disconnect minimum: 28 × 1.15 = 32.2 A — so the common 60 A disconnect is the shelf pick, and a 30 A disconnect fails this section even though it exceeds the running amps.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (not code): the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip at trim — the rating still comes from this section, and the breaker follows the nameplate under S-03.
sections.figure_idea: Disconnect rating card: RLA × 1.15 arrow to the next standard disconnect size.

sections.title: The HVAC disconnect — within sight and readily accessible
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.14 requires the disconnecting means for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to be within sight from the equipment and readily accessible to it, with an exception for certain industrial/process installations where conditions are met. 'Within sight' carries the Article 100 meaning: visible and within 50 ft. The disconnect may be on the equipment or separate from it, but a person servicing the unit must be able to reach it and see the unit from it. A breaker inside the house panel does not satisfy this by itself. The disconnect also may not be mounted on a panel that is designed to allow access to the equipment itself, and it may not be placed where it obscures the equipment nameplate.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 440.14: The A/C and refrigeration disconnect now has to have 110.26(A) working space, on top of the long-standing in-sight and readily accessible rules. The disconnect for A/C or refrigeration equipment must now have working space that meets 110.26(A).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Set the disconnect where the service tech stands: at the condenser pad, in sight, with working space in front of it, not behind a fence line or above reach. On a change-out, if the old disconnect is inside the old unit's shadow or was never installed, relocate or add it as part of the job and note it on the invoice record.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: exterior disconnects live in weather — use listed outdoor equipment and keep the working space clear of the condensate line and landscaping at final.

nec2023_change.change: The A/C and refrigeration disconnect now has to have 110.26(A) working space, on top of the long-standing in-sight and readily accessible rules. The disconnect for A/C or refrigeration equipment must now have working space that meets 110.26(A).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 440.14 A/C disconnect working space

sections.title: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a compressor circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.22 sizes the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a hermetic motor-compressor circuit and ties it to the equipment's rated-load or branch-circuit selection current, with the marked MOCP on a listed unit's nameplate being the number the installer works to in practice. As with motors generally, this device is allowed to be larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because equipment overload protection inside the unit does the running protection and the breaker must ride through compressor starting current. That allowance only exists inside Article 440's system — never borrow it for a general circuit.

The arithmetic behind the nameplate MOCP, from 440.22(A): the protective device is rated at not more than 175 percent of the compressor's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater. If a device at that rating will not carry the starting current, 440.22(A) lets the rating be increased where 175% will not carry the starting current, but not above 225%..

Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current takes protection at 20 × 1.75 = 35 A; if 35 A will not start it, the ceiling is 20 × 2.25 = 45 A. On listed equipment the manufacturer's printed MOCP already reflects this math, so the plate still governs — this arithmetic is for the compressor-only case and for checking a plate that looks wrong. 440.22(A) also sets a floor: the device may not be less than 125 percent of the rated-load current. (440.22(B) covers equipment with more than one motor or other loads.)
sections.on_the_job: If a condenser trips a breaker sized at or below its MOCP, the fault is in the equipment or the circuit, not in the arithmetic: measure starting and running current and inspect the contactor and conductors before anyone proposes a larger breaker. A breaker above the nameplate MOCP is never the fix.

sections.title: Conductor sizing for a single motor-compressor
sections.plain_explanation: Section 440.32 sizes conductors for a single hermetic motor-compressor at not less than 125 percent of the compressor's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater. On listed equipment the manufacturer has already done this work and printed it as the MCA, so the field rule and the nameplate rule agree: the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA. Where you are sizing from a compressor's own data rather than a unit plate, this section is the arithmetic behind the plate.
sections.on_the_job: When the plate is present, wire to the MCA and do not re-derive it. When the plate is missing or illegible on existing equipment, stop and get the data from the manufacturer rather than estimating from tonnage.

sections.title: Room air conditioners (440.60–440.65)
sections.plain_explanation: Part VII of Article 440 covers the cord-and-plug room air conditioner — the window and through-wall units a tenant or homeowner plugs in. The load rules are the ones that matter: a single room unit on a branch circuit of its own may not exceed 80 percent of that circuit's rating; where the same circuit also feeds lighting or other receptacles, the unit may not exceed 50 percent. Section 440.65 adds the plug protection: single-phase room units must have leakage-current detection (LCDI) or arc-fault protection in the attachment plug or cord — the fat plug with the test buttons is a requirement, not an accessory. 440.65 also allows a factory-installed heat-detecting circuit interrupter (HDCI) besides LCDI or AFCI on single-phase cord-and-plug room air conditioners, and Part VII covers room units rated not over 40A, 250V, single-phase (440.62(A)).
sections.on_the_job: A window unit tripping a shared bedroom circuit is usually the 50 percent rule announcing itself. The fix is a dedicated circuit under the 80 percent rule, not a bigger breaker on the shared circuit.
sections.figure_idea: Two bars: dedicated circuit — unit up to 80 percent; shared circuit — unit capped at 50 percent.

sections.title: Generators — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 445 covers generators themselves: their marking, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, and shutdown controls. The transfer equipment and the optional-standby-system rules that decide what a generator may feed live mainly in Chapter 7 (Article 702), and required standby systems in 700/701 — this article is about the machine. Sharma meets 445 on whole-house generator work in dwellings, where the 2020 outdoor shutdown rule on the next pages is the item inspectors ask about.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 445.18: A generator's disconnect can now sit inside the unit behind a hinged cover, provided a sign points to its location. The emergency shutdown rules moved out to 445.19. The disconnect can be inside the generator, behind a hinged door, cover or panel, as long as a sign meeting 110.21(B) shows where it is.
• 445.19: Generator shutdown rules moved to their own section, 445.19. Remote and dwelling shutdown switches can now mount on the generator enclosure, labeled "Generator Emergency Shutdown." The remote shutdown switch and the dwelling shutdown device can now mount on the outside of the generator enclosure.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Separate the two questions on a generator job: is the machine itself installed to 445, and is the system it feeds wired and sized to Chapter 7? Passing one does not pass the other. Cross-link to Chapter 7 for transfer-switch sizing; do not size a transfer switch from this chapter.

sections.title: Stationary generators must be listed (2020 addition)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.6, added in the 2020 edition, requires stationary generators operating at 600 volts or less to be listed. Before this edition a generator could arrive on a job with no listing requirement stated in Article 445 itself; now the machine's listing is a code item, checked the same way as any other equipment's. The listing carries the installation instructions that 110.3(B) makes enforceable, including clearances, exhaust, and the shutdown arrangement in 445.18.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 445.6: Stationary generators of any voltage now need a listing. The 2020 rule only reached units rated 600 volts or less. All stationary generators must be listed, whatever their voltage rating.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: At quote stage for a standby generator, confirm the exact model is listed and get its installation manual into the job file before the pad is poured. An unlisted or grey-market unit is a stop, not a discount.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: hurricane-season generator work is where unlisted units most often appear in Sharma's territory; the listing check happens at quote, not at inspection.

nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 445.6 Generator listing

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for generators (445.12)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 445.12 requires generators to be protected from overload — by inherent design, circuit breakers, fuses, or another identified means — so a fault or an overload cannot cook the machine that is supposed to be the backup. It works with 445.13, which sizes the conductors from the generator at 115 percent of nameplate current. Together they mean the generator's own protection and the wire leaving it are both chosen from the nameplate, and a transfer scheme never leaves the generator feeding a fault with nothing able to open.
sections.on_the_job: Read the generator nameplate for both numbers at the site survey: rated amps for the 445.13 conductor math, and the machine's built-in protection for the 445.12 check. Both go on the job record.
sections.figure_idea: Generator nameplate card with two callouts: rated amps (wire math) and built-in protection (overload check).

sections.title: Generator conductors — 115 percent of nameplate current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.13 sizes the conductors from a generator to its first distribution device or devices at not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, with the article's own provisions for cases where design prevents overloading. The margin exists because a generator can be asked to carry its full rating for the whole duration of an outage. Neutral conductor treatment has its own paragraphs in this section, so do not assume the neutral is automatically the same size as the ungrounded conductors on every system type.

Worked example: a 22 kW standby unit at 240 V single-phase has a nameplate current of about 92 A; 92 × 1.15 = 105.8 A minimum conductor ampacity — the feeder lands on conductors rated at least 106 A (2 AWG copper at the 75°C column is 115 A), with the overcurrent arrangement set by the generator and transfer equipment design.
sections.on_the_job: Size from the nameplate on the actual machine, and confirm whether the installation is a separately derived system before you settle the neutral and grounding arrangement — that decision belongs with the Chapter 2/Chapter 7 pages and the transfer equipment, and it changes this section's wiring.

sections.title: Outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one-family dwelling
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.18(D) is the 2020 provision the brief assigns to the emergency shutdown of a generator installed outdoors at a one- or two-family dwelling: in addition to the shutdown provisions that apply to generators generally, a dwelling unit generator located outside must have a readily accessible disconnecting/shutdown device located outside the dwelling, so the machine can be shut down by occupants or first responders without entering the building or standing at the machine itself. Read it together with the rest of 445.18, which governs shutdown of the prime mover generally.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 445.19: The emergency-shutdown rules moved from 445.18 to new 445.19; for one- and two-family dwellings the remote emergency shutdown must be outside the dwelling (445.19(C)). 445.18 now lets the generator disconnect sit inside the unit behind a cover if a 110.21(B) sign shows where it is.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a dwelling generator job, locate the outdoor shutdown where a responder would look for it — at the normal entry side of the house, plainly identified — and test it at start-up. Confirm the device you installed is the one the generator's listing and the AHJ expect; note its location on the job record and the panel directory.

nec2023_change.change: The emergency-shutdown rules moved from 445.18 to new 445.19; for one- and two-family dwellings the remote emergency shutdown must be outside the dwelling (445.19(C)). 445.18 now lets the generator disconnect sit inside the unit behind a cover if a 110.21(B) sign shows where it is.
nec2023_change.source: Georgia DCA 2023 NEC presentation; NYEIA 2020/2023 residential changes; Electrical Exam Coach 445.18

sections.title: Transformers and transformer vaults — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 450 covers transformers: overcurrent protection of the transformer and its conductors, location, guarding, ventilation, and the vault construction rules for indoor installations. Sharma's day-to-day contact is the small dry-type transformer in light commercial work — a 480-to-208/120 step-down or a control transformer — where the protection table and the primary/secondary conductor rules are the working content. Vault and liquid-filled rules are later-pass material for this book.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 450.2: 450.2 is no longer a definition. It's now a rule: each transformer must meet Article 450 on its own, unless a specific rule allows units to be tied together and run as one. Each transformer has to meet Article 450 by itself.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: For a dry-type install: confirm primary and secondary protection against the 450.3 table for the actual voltages, confirm the secondary conductors are protected as Chapter 2 requires, and keep ventilation clearances the listing demands. Photograph the transformer nameplate into the job file.

nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 450.2 Interconnected transformers

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 450.3 sets transformer overcurrent protection through its tables, one for transformers over 1000V and one for 1000V and below, with the required protection depending on voltage, whether protection is primary-only or primary-and-secondary, and the transformer's impedance where the table calls for it. Primary-only protection is permitted only within the table's limits; beyond them, both sides must be protected. The percentages are table lookups for the specific case — do not carry one remembered percentage to a different voltage or impedance.

The Table 450.3(B) rows (1000 V and below) that cover the dry-type work Sharma actually sets:
• Primary and secondary currents of 9 A or more, primary protection only — 125 percent of rated primary current
• Same size range, protection on both sides — primary up to 250 percent, secondary not over 125 percent
• Primary current under 9 A, primary protection only — up to 167 percent
• Primary current under 2 A, primary protection only — up to 300 percent
Where the calculated percentage falls between standard device ratings, the table's notes permit the next higher standard rating in the cases they cover.

Worked example: a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V transformer draws about 54 A on the primary; primary-only protection is 54 × 1.25 = 67.5 A, so a 70 A device is the standard pick.
sections.on_the_job: Work the table for the case in front of you and write the case (voltage class, impedance, primary-only or both) on the worksheet. If the impedance is not on the nameplate you can read, stop — the table answer may depend on it.

sections.title: Transformer ventilation — and no storage on top
sections.plain_explanation: Section 450.9 requires transformers to be installed so air can circulate and carry heat away, and the 2020 edition expanded its marking provisions so the horizontal top surfaces of covered dry-type transformers are marked against being used for storage. A transformer is a heater by design losses; blocking its vents or stacking boxes on it raises its temperature and shortens its life. Ventilation is an installation requirement, not a housekeeping preference.
sections.on_the_job: Keep the manufacturer's clearances on all vented faces and treat the top of a dry-type transformer as equipment space, never a shelf. On a commercial service call, photograph and report storage stacked on a transformer rather than just moving it quietly — it will be back.

sections.title: A transformer needs a disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation: Section 450.14 requires a disconnecting means for transformers, located either in a readily accessible location within sight of the transformer or in a remote location, with the article's exceptions (which include certain small transformers such as Class 2 and similar limited cases). Where the disconnect is remote, it must be lockable in the open position and the transformer must be marked with the disconnect's location, so a person servicing the transformer can find and secure its source. The 2020 clarifications to this section are about exactly that remote case.
sections.on_the_job: On a dry-type install, decide the disconnect location with the transformer location, not after. If the disconnect ends up remote, apply the lockable arrangement and the location marking in the same visit and record both in the job file.

sections.title: Where dry-type transformers may sit (450.21)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 450.21 governs indoor dry-type transformer locations. Transformers rated 112½ kVA or less must sit at least 12 inches from combustible material, unless separated from it by a fire-resistant, heat-insulated barrier, or enclosed so the heat stays in. Larger indoor dry-types — over 112½ kVA — go in a transformer room of fire-resistant construction, with the section's exceptions for enclosed units and higher insulation systems. Ventilation under 450.9 keeps the heat moving; this section keeps the heat away from things that burn.
sections.on_the_job: Setting a dry-type in a wood-framed electrical closet: measure the 12 inches before the transformer is hung, not after. The closet's wall finish decides which rule you are under — confirm what the wall is made of.

sections.title: Phase converters — article intro
sections.plain_explanation: Article 455 covers phase converters, the equipment that lets three-phase motors run from a single-phase supply. It addresses marking, conductor sizing for the single-phase input, and disconnect requirements, with sizing tied to the largest motor or load the converter serves. Sharma meets converters rarely, on small commercial and agricultural-type jobs at the edge of its territory; this first pass gives the article its place and scope.
sections.on_the_job: A converter is sized to its load, not to the building service. Get the motor data for everything the converter will ever run at once, and give that list to the office before quoting the install.

sections.title: Capacitors — article intro
sections.plain_explanation: Article 460 covers capacitors installed on electrical systems, most often for power-factor correction on commercial services and large motor loads. Its working rules concern conductor ampacity (capacitor circuits are sized above the capacitor's rated current), overcurrent protection, disconnecting means, and the stored-energy discharge that makes a capacitor keep a charge after it is switched off. That stored charge is the safety point of the article: a disconnected capacitor is not automatically a dead capacitor.
sections.on_the_job: Treat capacitor terminals as live until discharged and verified with a meter. Allow the discharge device its time, then test — never assume. Include the capacitor's kvar and voltage from its nameplate in the job record.

sections.title: Resistors and reactors — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 470 covers resistors and reactors used on electrical systems, such as starting resistors for motors and current-limiting reactors. Its themes are clearance from combustible material (these devices make heat by design), enclosure and guarding, and conductor sizing for the duty. Sharma encounters this equipment mainly inside larger commercial gear rather than as field-installed material, so this first pass is a scope page.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 470.2: Made new Section 470.2 the placeholder for reconditioned equipment, indicating that reconditioning of a resistor is not permitted and that reactors shall follow manufacturers' guidelines.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Heat is the installation: keep the clearances and ventilation the listing requires, and do not enclose a resistor bank in a way its manufacturer did not intend. If a reactor or resistor shows heat discoloration on a service call, report it rather than just resetting the equipment.

sections.title: Storage batteries — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 480 covers storage battery installations: the battery systems that back up services, feed UPS equipment, and increasingly pair with solar and generator work. Its working rules address disconnecting means, overcurrent protection, wiring to battery circuits, and the ventilation and spill concerns that depend on battery chemistry. The article works alongside the energy-storage rules in Chapter 7 (Article 706), which govern the system as a whole — 480 is about the battery installation itself.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 480.1: Article 480 is now Stationary Standby Batteries and covers only standby battery systems over 1 kWh. Smaller ones, like a fire alarm panel battery, fall outside it. Article 480 now applies only to stationary standby batteries with more than 1 kWh (3.6 MJ) of capacity.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Identify the chemistry and the system listing before you wire anything: vented, sealed, and lithium systems have different room and protection needs. Put the battery disconnect where it is identified for the system and label it at the service as the system rules require (see Chapter 7 cross-links).
sections.florida_note: Florida note: battery rooms and garages in Florida heat age batteries faster; record the install date and chemistry in the job file so replacement is planned, not discovered during an outage.

sections.title: Battery disconnects — DC is its own problem
sections.plain_explanation: Section 480.7 sets the disconnecting methods for battery circuits, reorganized and expanded in the 2020 edition as battery requirements were gathered back into Article 480 from Article 706. The field point that matters most: interrupting DC is harder than interrupting AC, because DC has no natural current zero to help an arc die. A switching device must be rated for the DC voltage and current it will actually break; an AC-only device is not assumed suitable, whatever its amp rating says.
sections.on_the_job: Read the DC rating on any battery disconnect, fuse holder, or breaker before it goes in, and confirm polarity markings on polarized DC devices. If the rating plate does not mention DC, the device does not go on a battery circuit.

sections.title: Battery interconnections (moved into 480 in 2020)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 480.12 carries the battery interconnection requirements that the 2020 edition moved into Article 480 from Article 706: the conductors and connections that join cells and batteries into a bank, sized for the maximum current the bank can deliver and made with terminals and methods suited to the battery system. Battery banks can deliver enormous fault current at very low impedance, so connection quality — correct lugs, correct torque, protected runs — is a safety item, not a neatness item. Manufacturer instructions for the specific battery system govern the details the article leaves to the listing.
sections.on_the_job: Torque interconnection hardware to the battery manufacturer's specification and record it; a loose intercell connection announces itself as heat under load. Keep interconnection runs protected from physical damage and from the electrolyte environment of the battery type installed.

sections.title: Equipment over 1000 volts, nominal — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 490 covers equipment operating over 1000 volts nominal: medium-voltage switchgear, conductors' termination practices, and clearances for the gear Sharma's crews do not normally install but may work around on commercial and utility-adjacent sites. It closes Chapter 4 in official order. Nothing in Sharma's residential work is installed under this article, and no Sharma field employee works on over-1000V equipment under this book — such work is referred to qualified medium-voltage contractors.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 490: Article 490 was renumbered as Article 495, 'Equipment Over 1000 Volts ac, 1500 Volts dc, Nominal'; 490.21 equipment-specific provisions were deleted/relocated.
• Article 495: All the requirements previously found in Article 490, Equipment Over 1000 Volts, Nominal, have been moved to Article 495.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Your job with 490 equipment is recognition and respect: identify it, keep clear of it, and never open, rack, or test it. If a job appears to require work on the medium-voltage side, stop and take it to Sanjay and Mike the same day.
